longer in a historical but in an analytical way. All monetary wealth comes only
from the transformation of Work into Money, the Work itself coming from the
previous transformation of heat. The above presentation of the two
transformations exhorts us to consider the economic one of the same essence as
the physical one, i.e. thermomechanical.
The analogy between these two transformations (thermomechanical and
economic) can be accentuated as the following operational sequences present it:

In physics, the greatest possible temperature difference is sought,

in Economy, the greatest possible difference in Utility is sought.
It should be noted that the work that is the consequence of the thermodynamic
transformation (transformation 1) becomes (partially) the cause of the economic
transformation (transformation 2).
However, the availability of mechanical energy is a function of the cost of
thermal energy, and in particular the cost of fossil fuels. The lower the price of
fuels, the more cheaply mechanical work can be produced and hence the Product
produced. But then, the share of manpower costs in the cost price of the Product
increases as the cost price of energy decreases. This leads to an increase in the
trend towards the elimination of manpower (relocation, replacement of manpower
by motors and machines, redundancies, etc.).
It is therefore possible to write the following two sequences respectively with
economic and physical characters :
1.
Decrease in energy prices ⇒ decrease in the cost price ⇒
increase in the share of manpower costs ⇒ increase in the
propensity to crowd out local wage earners ⇒ increase in
local unemployment ⇒ increase in inequality.
2.
Decrease in energy prices ⇒ increase in available work ⇒
increase in the speed of production ⇒ increase in the
number of products produced ⇒ increase in waste ⇒
increase in environmental degradation.

observations: 204
The effective period begins in 1990 because the merged selected series do not
provide a complete 1965-2023 overlap for the chosen indicators and countries.
4.2 Reconstruction formula
Energy use is reconstructed as:
energy = gdp_ppp_real / gdp_per_energy
This is dimensionally coherent. If:
gdp_ppp_real = PPP dollars
gdp_per_energy = PPP dollars per kg oil equivalent
then:
energy = PPP dollars / (PPP dollars per kg oil equivalent)
= kg oil equivalent
This corrects an earlier weaker construction that divided market-price GDP by a
PPP-based GDP-per-energy ratio. The corrected construction is not equivalent
to using a fully independent physical-energy series, but it is internally coherent.
4.3 Models
For each country or aggregate, three OLS models are estimated.
Level model:
GDP_i,t = alpha_i + beta_i Energy_i,t + epsilon_i,t
Log-log model:
log(GDP_i,t) = alpha_i + beta_i log(Energy_i,t) + epsilon_i,t
Annual log-change model:
Delta log(GDP_i,t) = alpha_i + beta_i Delta log(Energy_i,t) + epsilon_i,t
The level model is intuitive but sensitive to common trends. The log-log model
provides an elasticity. The annual log-change model is more demanding because
it tests whether yearly changes move together, not merely whether two variables
trend upward over time.

text:
The run metadata reports 204 observations across six country or area codes: WLD, USA,
FRA, DEU, CHN, and IND.
Energy is reconstructed as:
energy = gdp_ppp_real / gdp_per_energy
This replaces the earlier, weaker construction:
energy = gdp_market_real / gdp_per_energy
The earlier version mixed market-dollar GDP with a PPP-based GDP-per-energy ratio.
The updated reconstruction is dimensionally coherent because both numerator and
denominator are expressed in PPP terms.
This remains a reconstructed energy-use proxy, not an independently downloaded
physical energy series. This limitation is discussed below.
4
Method
For each country or aggregate, the script estimates three ordinary least squares spec-
ifications.
4.1
Level regression
GDP_i,t = α_i + β_i Energy_i,t + ε_i,t
This regression captures the long-run level association between real GDP and recon-
structed energy use. It is visually intuitive but vulnerable to common trends.
4.2
Log-log regression
log(GDP_i,t) = α_i + β_i log(Energy_i,t) + ε_i,t
The coefficient β is interpreted as a long-run elasticity. For example, β = 1.6 means
that, within the observed historical relationship, a 1% increase in reconstructed en-
ergy use is associated with approximately a 1.6% increase in real GDP.
This is not a causal claim.
4.3
Annual log-change regression
Δlog(GDP_i,t) = α_i + β_i Δlog(Energy_i,t) + ε_i,t
This specification is more demanding. It tests whether yearly changes in GDP and
yearly changes in energy use move together, rather than merely showing that two
variables trend upward over several decades.
